blocks.prompt: The Fox That Hunts by Ear
blocks.text: A fox does not need to see a mouse to catch it. It needs to hear one. A fox has tall ears that turn like little cups. It stands very still in the snow. Its ears move. It is listening for a soft scratch under the snow. When the fox knows where the mouse is, it jumps. It jumps high, then dives down nose first. The snow is deep, but the fox has already worked out the spot. At night the fox curls up in a ball. It wraps its bushy tail around its nose to stay warm. The tip of that tail is white.

blocks.prompt: The Dog That Hunts Like a Cat
blocks.text: A fox is a dog that behaves like a cat. Foxes belong to the dog family, along with wolves and pet dogs. But a wolf hunts in a pack, and a fox hunts alone. That one difference changed the whole animal. A wolf can chase a deer for miles because it has help. A fox is small. Under all that fur it weighs about as much as a house cat, and it has nobody to help it. So the fox does not chase. It creeps. It freezes. It waits with its ears turning, and then it pounces, exactly like a cat on a lawn. Look closer and the cat keeps showing up. A fox has narrow pupils that close into a slit, which most dogs do not have. It has stiff whiskers on its face, and more whiskers partway down its front legs, so it can feel what it has caught even in the dark. In America, the gray fox goes further and climbs trees. It is still a dog. It just found a cat's way of making a living.

notes: Red fox: Vulpes vulpes

blocks.prompt: How a Fox Finds a Mouse It Cannot See
blocks.text: A red fox standing still in a snowy field is doing something remarkable, and from the outside it looks like nothing at all. The mouse is under the snow. The fox cannot see it and cannot smell much through the frozen crust. All it has is sound. Foxes hear low sounds better than almost any other hunter their size, and low is exactly what a small animal makes when it shuffles through dead grass or scratches at the wall of its tunnel. Those tall ears swivel one at a time. The tiny difference between what the left ear hears and what the right ear hears tells the fox where the mouse is standing, to within a few inches, under a blanket it cannot see through. Then comes the strange part. The fox rears onto its back legs and throws itself into the air, sometimes higher than a person's waist, and drops nose first through the crust with its front paws tucked beside its jaw. It is aiming at a target it has never once laid eyes on. Scientists in the Czech Republic spent years recording these leaps. They noticed something nobody expected. When the fox could not see its prey, it tended to line itself up facing roughly north before it jumped, and those north facing leaps succeeded far more often than leaps in any other direction. One idea is that the fox is somehow reading the Earth's magnetic field, using it like a compass to judge the distance to a sound. Nobody has proved it yet. It is one of the best unanswered questions about an animal most of us walk straight past.

the small difference between what each ear hears tells it the direction and distance

(inference: it separates what is known from what is still a guess, which keeps the writing honest)

notes: The most widespread wild carnivore on Earth
Native across the whole northern half of the world

blocks.prompt: The Fox That Moved to Town
blocks.text: No wild meat eater on Earth lives in more places than the red fox. It hunts above the Arctic Circle, where the ground stays frozen most of the year. It hunts at the dry edges of the Sahara. It lives in the forests of Japan, the farmland of France, the hills of Afghanistan, and the back streets of Chicago and London. In the 1850s, settlers shipped red foxes to Australia so they would have something to chase on horseback. Within about seventy years the foxes had spread across most of the continent, eating their way through small native animals that had never encountered a predator like them and had no idea what to do. Why does the fox win everywhere? Because it is not fussy. A wolf needs large prey and a great deal of empty space. A panda needs bamboo. A fox needs almost nothing in particular. It eats mice, rabbits, beetles, earthworms, birds, eggs, blackberries, windfall apples, and, in a city, whatever ends up on the sidewalk. When it finds more food than it can eat, it digs a hole, buries the surplus, and comes back later, and it remembers where. Its chest is narrow, so it slips through a gap barely wider than its own head. Its den can be a hole it dug, a hole something else dug, the dark under a shed, or the space beneath a set of steps. That is why the fox came to town. Not because it grew fond of us, and not because anyone invited it. A city is warm. It is full of scraps. Nobody hunts a fox on a street corner, and there are a thousand quiet gaps to sleep in. City foxes now live on much smaller patches of ground than country foxes, because they never have to walk far to eat. It is worth sitting with what that means. The fox did not change itself to fit our world. It was already, long before we built anything, exactly the animal our cities would reward.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Fox That Hunts by Ear

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A silver fox is a red fox with black fur
Dmitri Belyaev began the fox experiment in 1959
Site: Novosibirsk, Siberia
Bred on one rule only: calmness toward a human hand
Lyudmila Trut ran the study for decades after
In 2020 other researchers challenged what it proves

blocks.prompt: The Foxes That Were Supposed to Explain Dogs
blocks.text: In 1959, a Russian scientist named Dmitri Belyaev began an experiment on a fur farm in Siberia, and the animal he chose was the fox. The question underneath it was really about dogs. Every dog alive descends from wolves, but the change from wolf to dog is baffling. Dogs do not merely behave differently from wolves. They look different. Floppy ears, curled tails, blotchy white coats, shorter faces. Nobody ever bred a wolf for floppy ears, and yet tame animals all over the world keep arriving at the same odd collection of features. Pigs, goats, rabbits, horses, and cows each show pieces of the same pattern. Belyaev's insight was that you could not answer this by studying dogs, because dogs finished changing thousands of years ago. You would have to start again, with an animal nobody had tamed, and watch it happen in real time. So he took silver foxes, which are red foxes born with black fur, and he bred them on one rule and one rule only. Each generation, a worker opened a cage and offered a hand. Foxes that snapped or cowered were not bred. The calmest few were. No one selected for looks. No one selected for ear shape, tail curl, or coat pattern. Calmness was the only thing ever chosen, generation after generation, in the cold outside Novosibirsk. The foxes changed quickly. Within roughly ten generations some of them whimpered for attention, licked hands, and wagged their tails when a person approached. Then the uninvited things arrived. Floppy ears. Curled tails. White patches across the face. Shorter snouts. Animals breeding at strange times of year. Belyaev appeared to have caught domestication in the act, compressed from millennia into decades, and his colleague Lyudmila Trut kept the work running for the rest of the century. It is a beautiful result. It may also be less tidy than it sounds. In 2020, a group of researchers examined where Belyaev's foxes had actually come from. They were not wild. They had been bought from fur farms on Prince Edward Island in Canada, where foxes had already been bred in captivity for around fifty years, and where farmers had long been quietly favoring whichever animals were easiest to handle. Records and photographs from those farms show foxes with floppy ears and patchy coats before the Siberian experiment ever began. If those traits were already sitting in the population, then the experiment did not conjure them out of tameness. It concentrated what was there. The Siberian foxes are still real. They are still tame, still extraordinary, still unlike any wild fox. What is in dispute is not the foxes. It is what they prove. And that is not a failure of science. That is science working exactly as intended: a gorgeous story gets told, someone goes back and checks the paperwork, and the story comes back smaller and truer than before.
